params.text: Value is the term we use to describe the range of lightness or darkness of a visual element. Notice below how we move from a dark value on the left to a lighter value on the right.

Value does not have to just be black and white, though it is easier to see the value when it is. A single color can also have a range of values by adjusting its TINT percentage in InDesign. Below are the various tints of Pantone Solid Coated 647. From left to right: 100%, 80%, 60%, 40%, 20%, and 0%.

params.alt: various tints of Pantone Solid Coated 647

params.text: Value can also be present when using different colors in a design. Remember, value is the lighter or darker quality of an element.

params.alt: yellow text on blue background that reads This yellow text has a lighter value than the darker valued blue background.

params.text: Every design must have some contrast (difference) in value. The minute you put black text on a white page, you have a contrast of value (dark text on a light background). Even light gray text on a white background has a contrast in value. However, when you look at the following, which has the greater contrast (difference) in value?

params.question: Which of the above has the highest contrast or difference in value? In other words, a strong difference between light vs dark.

params.text:
The darker element on a lighter background has a higher contrast (difference). High contrast makes elements stand out more easily from each other.

The lighter text on the right has a low contrast (difference). This can cause elements to be difficult to read because they appear to be almost the same value (light vs. dark) as the background. Keep this in mind when working with important information that must be read or elements that must stand out.

params.alt: Two texts showcasing ease of use in reading for higher contrast of light text on dark background

params.text: A good use of value can create both a visual and emotional effect. A use of lower range contrast can give your design a softer look and feel or be very subtle, like the wedding invitation on the left. Whereas a higher range of contrast is bold and attention grabbing, like the wedding invitation on the right.

metadata.title: High vs Low Contrast in Value
metadata.extraTitle: High vs Low Contrast in Value

params.text:
Most beginning designers find it difficult to utilize value successfully in their design. Most avoid high contrast or low contrast with shades or fading because they are simply unaware of the power value can have in a design. 

When you want to watch fireworks, which is a better setting? The day or night? If you launch fireworks during the day, there is not enough contrast in value between the bright fireworks and bright sky to really stand out. Their impact gets lost within the background of the lighter valued sky. At night, however, you have the perfect contrast to draw the attention to the brightly colored fireworks. 

In a design, the “fireworks” or important information you want your audience to read must have a high enough contrast to be easily seen. 

Take a look at the following ads by Coca Cola. Notice how they use a high contrast of white on red in the first and third add to a strong visual interest. In the middle, they use of the contrast in value between the darker hands and the light background to create the shape of coke bottle.

The opposite of such bold high contrast is the more subtle low contrast. Did you know that Navy ships are painted gray due to the fact that the color gray (or haze gray) reduces the value contrast of the boat against the horizon, making it tougher to be spotted by the enemy? It helps it to blend into the background sky.

When you want something in your design to still be present but very subtle, use a lower contrast in value. This will fade your element to the background.

Select the information icons in the image below to see how elements with a low contrast in value were used in the designs.

The designer uses faint (lighter value/low contrast) text to help add to the background without it being overpowering. While it is something you notice, it is subtle and is not the first thing that grabs your eye. This is a great technique when working with textures or if you feel your background space needs something. Faint text is great for that.

When you look at this flyer, which text do you see first? Probably the white. That is because the white elements are the more important elements in the poster. To bring those elements forward, the designer chose to use a blue similar in value to the background to help push the other text information backwards. It's still there and readable, but it is more subtle than the bolder white text.

metadata.title: Value can have a powerful influence
metadata.extraTitle: Value can have a powerful influence

params.text:
As a designer, you must be able to recognize when you have enough contrast in your values to make sure the information that needs to be read can be. Recall the element of value is immediate the moment you add any element to a medium. Whether or not it is high value (lighter) or low value (darker) is dependent on the element in relation to others, including the background. 

Take a look at the following billboard by Chipotle. Look at how they use a combination of both high value (lighter) and low value (darker) text to drive their point home and get you to focus on the key message.

Chipotle uses high value (lighter) text as really a background element to their main message. Only foot traffic may really have the time to stop and read it. 

Though this is high value (lighter) text, we would also say it has a low contrast (difference) in value as the text is very near the same high value as the background.

Chipotle uses low value (darker) text against a high value background element to make sure the key point stands out, "Our Ingrediants Are Better."

Though this is low value (darker) text, we would also say it has a high contrast (difference) in value as the text is much darker than the high value background.

params.text: With programs like InDesign, Illustrator, and Photoshop, the value of elements can always be adjusted from 1-100% using Opacity in the Properties > Appearance panel.
When working with a single color, you can control the value by adjusting the tint, screen, or intensity of the color.

params.alt: Controlling a single color tint in InDesign

params.text:
You can also choose completely different colors that are either similar or different in value, depending on the effect you are looking for (similar values for faded background different values for elements that need to be easily seen or read). 

A recommendation is to always print a grayscale proof copy to make sure your colors have enough contrast for elements that must be read. Trust, just because you have a contrast (difference) in color, does not necessarily mean you have a contrast in value.

params.alt: yellow on blue in grayscale looks good. Green on blue in grayscale does not.

params.text: The correct value is whichever one supports your design and helps your message to be read clearly.
